geo.title: What to know
geo.body:
Practice the lessons so far, then check your answers.

Goal: I can apply SAS, ASA, and the isosceles theorems.

  • 4.1 I can write a congruence statement with matching vertices.
  • 4.2 I can test which sets of three parts build only one triangle.
  • 4.3 I can explain why SAS follows from the definition of congruence.
  • 4.4 I can explain why ASA follows from rigid motions.
  • 4.5 I can write a proof using SAS or ASA.
  • 4.6 I can use congruent triangles to prove parts equal.
  • 4.7 I can prove that base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal.
  • 4.8 I can prove the converse of the Isosceles Triangle Theorem and its corollaries.
  • 4.10 I can follow and explain a proof of SSS using SAS and isosceles triangles, covering every case of where the joining segment falls.
  • 4.11 I can give a counterexample showing SSA is not a congruence test.
  • 4.12 I can construct a congruent triangle and justify it with SSS or SAS.
  • 4.13 I can use congruent triangles to prove why bisector constructions work.
  • 4.14 I can choose a strategy for a congruence proof.

slides.title: Practice: 4.1
slides.html: Triangle PQR is congruent to triangle XYZ. Which side matches QR? Which angle matches angle P?
slides.reveal: YZ matches QR; angle X matches angle P.

slides.title: Practice: 4.4
slides.html: In the ASA argument, why does C have to land exactly on F?
slides.reveal: C lies on both ray DF and ray EF, and two rays that are not on the same line meet in at most one point, which is F.

slides.title: Practice: 4.7
slides.html: An isosceles triangle has a vertex angle of 40 degrees. What do you know about its base angles now? (Angle sum waits for Unit 5.)
slides.reveal: They are equal to each other. Once we prove the 180 degree sum, each will be 70 degrees.

slides.title: Common traps
slides.html:
Watch out for these common mistakes:

  • SSA (and AAA) prove congruence
  • corresponding parts can be matched in any order
  • CPCTC can be used before triangles are proved congruent
